note.title: Current and voltage rules in series and parallel circuits
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Series: the current is the same through every component
Series: the voltages across the components add up to the supply voltage
Parallel: the voltage across every branch is the supply voltage
Parallel: the current in the main line is the sum of the branch currents
Unequal branches: each branch's current is the supply voltage divided by its own resistance (V = I R)

notOnThisSpec: Calculating the combined resistance of resistors in series or parallel (that is the next topic)
Potential dividers, variable-resistor circuits, LDRs and thermistors
Kirchhoff's laws by name, and internal resistance
Potential difference as the required word (CCEA says voltage)

mustBeAbleTo: Decide whether a circuit is series or parallel by tracing the route from the cell back to the cell
State that in series the current is the same through every component
State that in series the voltages across the components add up to the supply voltage, and find a missing one
State that in parallel the voltage across every branch is the supply voltage
State that in parallel the current in the main line is the sum of the branch currents, and find a missing one
Complete a grid of ammeter and voltmeter readings from two readings given
Share a current between equal branches, and (Higher paper) between unequal branches: I = V ÷ R for each, or twice the resistance takes half the current
Explain why the lights in a house are wired in parallel
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes, 70 marks at Foundation and 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. The rules are set as readings: a battery with two equal resistors in parallel, three ammeters and three voltmeters, two readings given and four to complete for a mark each (Summer 2019 Higher, Summer 2026 Foundation); ammeters in the main line either side of the branches (Summer 2022); a resistor feeding an equal parallel pair with one branch current in milliamps (Summer 2021 Foundation); on the Higher paper, currents shared between unequal resistors with only the total given (Summer 2021, Summer 2023). The rules then feed a three- or four-mark V = I R calculation on the same circuit.
traps: Splitting the current equally between branches that are not equal: the smaller resistance takes the larger share, I = V ÷ R for each branch (Summer 2023 P2 Higher Q6)
Putting a current in milliamps straight into V = I R: convert to amps on its own line first (Summer 2023 P2 Higher Q6; Summer 2025 P2 Higher Q3)
Starting the follow-on calculation from a wrong form of V = I R, such as R = I ÷ V, which scores nothing (Summer 2024 P2 Foundation Q7, Higher Q4)

Giving a series component the whole supply voltage: only parallel branches each get the supply; in series the voltages share it (the six-meter grid shape of Summer 2019 Higher and Summer 2026 Foundation)

steps.working: Z carries the same current as Y: 45 mA.
steps.decision: Y and Z are equal and sit between the same two junctions, so they have the same voltage across them and take the same current.

options: Because equal resistors with the same voltage across them carry equal currents
Because the current through Z is whatever is left after Y
Because Z is nearer the cell
whyMenu.explain: The two branches share the same pair of junctions, so the voltage across each is the same; with equal resistances, I = V ÷ R gives equal currents. Nothing is left over: the junction splits the current between them equally.

steps.working: X carries both branch currents: 45 + 45 = 90 mA.
steps.decision: X is in the main line, so it carries the sum of the branch currents.
V = I R needs the current in amps. Convert before substituting, on its own line, so the examiner can see it.
Multiply the current through X by the resistance of X. The current and the resistance must belong to the same component.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: Z: 45 mA; X: 90 mA; voltage across X: 1.8 V.

items.stem: Before we start (you have met this already): an ammeter is to measure the current through a lamp. Where does it go?
items.skill: Prerequisite: meter positions (conductors, circuits and symbols)

options.text: in series with the lamp, in the same loop
options.feedback: In series. The current it measures has to pass through it.

options.text: in parallel, on its own branch across the lamp
options.feedback: That is the voltmeter's place. An ammeter goes in the loop, in series, so the lamp's current passes through it.

options.text: across the two terminals of the cell
options.feedback: Across the terminals is where a voltmeter measures the supply. An ammeter sits in the loop so that the current passes through it.

items.stem: Before we start (from Ohm's law): a 6 V supply is connected across a 12 Ω resistor. What current flows?

options.text: 2 A
options.feedback: That divides the resistance by the voltage. Current is voltage divided by resistance: 6 ÷ 12 = 0.50 A.
That multiplies. V = I R rearranges to I = V ÷ R: 6 ÷ 12 = 0.50 A.

items.stem: Before we start (from Ohm's law): a current is 250 mA. What is that in amps?

options.feedback: There are 1000 mA in 1 A, so 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.25 A.
That divides by 10. A milliamp is a thousandth of an amp, so divide by 1000: 0.25 A.
That multiplies by 1000, making the current bigger. A milliamp is smaller than an amp: 250 mA = 0.25 A.

items.stem: In a series circuit an ammeter just before a lamp reads 0.60 A. What does an ammeter just after the lamp read?

options.text: the same, 0.60 A
options.feedback: Yes. One loop, one current: the lamp takes energy from the charge, not charge from the current.

options.text: less, because the lamp has used some of the current
options.feedback: Current is not used up. Charge cannot vanish inside a lamp: whatever flows in flows out, so the two readings are equal.

options.text: more, because the current speeds up after the lamp
options.feedback: The current is the same at every point of a series loop. Nothing adds to it after a component.

items.stem: A 3 V supply drives a 5 Ω resistor and a 15 Ω resistor in parallel. The main line carries 0.80 A. What current flows in the 5 Ω resistor?

options.feedback: Yes. Each branch has 3 V across it, so 3 ÷ 5 = 0.60 A.
That halves the main-line current, which is only right for equal branches. The 5 Ω branch takes 3 ÷ 5 = 0.60 A, three times the other branch's share.
That is the current in the 15 Ω branch. The smaller resistance takes the larger current: 3 ÷ 5 = 0.60 A.

items.stem: Two components are in series with a 6 V supply. The voltmeter across the first reads 2.0 V. What does a voltmeter across the second read?

options.feedback: Yes. The readings add up to the supply: 6 − 2 = 4.0 V.
That gives the second component the whole supply, which is the parallel rule. In series the supply is shared out: the two readings add up to 6 V, so the second is 4.0 V.
That copies the first reading. Series voltages are only equal when the components are identical; here they must add up to 6 V, so the second is 4.0 V.

items.stem: Two lamps are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. What is the voltage across each lamp?
items.skill: Parallel: every branch gets the supply voltage

options.feedback: Yes. Each branch is connected straight across the battery, so each lamp has the full battery voltage.

options.text: 6 V
options.feedback: That shares the battery voltage between the lamps, which is the series rule. In parallel each branch sits across the battery and has the full 12 V.
Each branch is across the same battery, so each lamp has 12 V, no more: a voltage is not added once for every branch.

items.stem: Ammeter A1 in the main line of a parallel circuit reads 0.60 A. Ammeter A2 on one branch reads 0.25 A. What does ammeter A3 on the other branch read?
items.skill: Parallel: the currents add at the junction

options.feedback: Yes. What flows in flows out: 0.6 − 0.25 = 0.35 A.
That adds the branch to the main line. The main line feeds both branches, so the second branch is what is left: 0.6 − 0.25 = 0.35 A.
That halves the main-line current, which assumes the branches are equal. A2 shows they are not: the other branch takes 0.6 − 0.25 = 0.35 A.

parts.stem: Which statement explains why the three ammeters read the same?

options.text: there is only one route, so the same charge passes every point each second
options.feedback: Yes. One loop, one current, at every point.

options.text: the lamps share the current equally between them
options.feedback: Sharing between branches belongs to parallel circuits. In one loop nothing splits: the same current passes both lamps in turn.

options.text: the cell pushes the same amount of current into each lamp
options.feedback: The cell does not send a separate current to each lamp. One current flows round the whole loop and through both lamps in turn.

scheme.for: one route / one loop, so the same current passes every point

parts.workedSolution: There is only one route, so the charge that passes one lamp must pass the other; the same charge passes every point each second.

hints: Each branch is connected straight across the battery.
parts.stem: The battery voltage is 4.5 V. State the voltage across each lamp.
parts.workedSolution: 4.5 V. Every branch of a parallel circuit has the supply voltage across it; nothing is shared out between branches.

hints: Identical lamps with the same voltage across them take identical shares of the main-line current.
parts.stem: The ammeter in the main line reads 0.60 A. Calculate the current through one lamp.
parts.workedSolution: The three lamps are identical and each has 4.5 V across it, so they take equal currents: 0.6 ÷ 3 = 0.20 A.

hints: Ask what happens to the voltage across a branch that has not been touched.
parts.stem: One lamp is removed from its holder. What happens to the other two lamps?

options.text: they stay as bright, because each branch still has the full battery voltage
options.feedback: Yes. Each branch is its own route across the battery, so the others are untouched.

options.text: they get brighter, because the current no longer has to be shared three ways
options.feedback: The voltage across each branch is fixed by the battery, so each remaining lamp draws the same current as before and is exactly as bright.

options.text: they go out, because the circuit is broken
options.feedback: Only the removed lamp's branch is broken. The other branches are still complete routes from one terminal to the other.

scheme.for: unchanged / stay as bright: each branch still has the full supply voltage

parts.workedSolution: They stay as bright. Each remaining lamp is still connected straight across the battery, so the voltage across it, and the current through it, are unchanged.

context.setting: A string of 20 identical lamps connected in series to the 230 V mains

hints: In series the lamp voltages add up to the supply, and identical lamps take identical shares.
parts.stem: A string of decorative lights has 20 identical lamps connected in series to the 230 V mains. Calculate the voltage across each lamp.
parts.workedSolution: The 20 voltages add up to 230 V and the lamps are identical, so each takes 230 ÷ 20 = 11.5 V.

hints: However many lamps there are, a series string is still one loop.
parts.stem: The current through the first lamp is 0.25 A. State the current through the last lamp in the string.
parts.workedSolution: 0.25 A. The string is one loop, so the same current passes through every lamp.

hints: How many routes does a series string have?
parts.stem: The filament of one lamp breaks. What happens to the other lamps?

options.text: they all go out, because the only route round the circuit is broken
options.feedback: Yes. A series string has one route, so a single break stops the current everywhere.

options.text: they get brighter, because each now has a larger share of the voltage
options.feedback: A broken filament is a gap in the only loop, so no current flows through any lamp at all and none of them lights.

options.text: they stay lit, because each lamp has its own route to the mains
options.feedback: That is true of a parallel circuit. In series there is only one route, and a break anywhere breaks it for every lamp.

scheme.for: all go out: the single loop is broken, so no current flows

parts.workedSolution: They all go out. A series circuit has only one route, so a break anywhere stops the current through every lamp.

hints: Equal resistors with the same voltage across them take equal shares.
parts.stem: The two resistors are equal. Ammeter A1 reads 1.40 A. State the reading on ammeter A2.
parts.workedSolution: 0.70 A. The two branches are equal, so each takes half of 1.40 A.

hints: The other equal branch takes the other equal share.
parts.stem: State the reading on ammeter A3.
parts.workedSolution: 0.70 A. The second branch is identical, so it carries the same current as the first.

hints: Where the branches meet, their currents add back together.
parts.stem: State the reading on ammeter A4, in the main line after the two branches have joined again.
parts.workedSolution: 1.40 A. The branch currents add back together where the branches meet: 0.7 + 0.7 = 1.40 A, the same as A1.

hints: Equal resistors with the same voltage across them carry equal currents.
parts.stem: Resistors Y and Z are equal. A current of 30 mA flows through Y. State the current through Z, in milliamps.
parts.workedSolution: 30 mA. Y and Z are equal and have the same voltage across them, so they carry the same current.

hints: X is in the main line, so it carries both branch currents.
parts.stem: State the current through resistor X, in milliamps.
parts.workedSolution: 60 mA. X carries the two branch currents added together: 30 + 30 = 60 mA.

hints: There are 1000 milliamps in one amp, so divide by 1000.

commonErrors.feedback: 60 is the number of milliamps. An amp is 1000 milliamps, so divide by 1000: 0.06 A. Summer 2023 Higher candidates lost marks by using 600 mA as if it were 600 A.
Dividing by 10 is not enough: there are 1000 milliamps in an amp, so 60 mA = 0.06 A.
Dividing by 100 is not enough: there are 1000 milliamps in an amp, so 60 mA = 0.06 A.

parts.stem: Write the current through resistor X in amps.

hints: Use the current through X in amps, from part (c), with the resistance of X.

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies the milliamps by the ohms. V = I R needs the current in amps: 0.06 × 50 = 3.0 V. A reading of thousands of volts from a small cell is the sign a conversion was missed.

parts.stem:
Resistor X has a resistance of 50 Ω. Calculate the voltage across X.
Show your working out.

hints: Each branch is connected straight across the supply.
parts.stem: The supply voltage is 12.0 V. State the voltage across the 48 Ω resistor.
parts.workedSolution: 12.0 V. Every branch of a parallel circuit has the supply voltage across it, whatever its resistance.

hints: The branches are not equal, so do not halve. Use the voltage across the branch and its own resistance.

commonErrors.feedback: That halves the main-line current, which is only right when the two branches are equal. These are not: each branch takes the supply voltage divided by its own resistance, 12 ÷ 24 = 0.50 A. Summer 2023 Higher examiners found only the most able could do this when one resistance was twice the other.
That is the current in the 48 Ω branch. The 24 Ω resistor has the smaller resistance, so it takes the larger current: 12 ÷ 24 = 0.50 A.

parts.stem: The ammeter in the main line reads 0.75 A. Calculate the current through the 24 Ω resistor.
parts.workedSolution: Each branch has 12.0 V across it, so I = V ÷ R = 12 ÷ 24 = 0.50 A.

hints: Either divide the supply voltage by this branch's resistance, or take the first branch away from the main-line reading.

commonErrors.feedback: Half the main-line current is only right for equal branches. The 48 Ω branch has double the other branch's resistance, so it takes half as much current: 12 ÷ 48 = 0.25 A.
That is the current in the 24 Ω branch. The larger resistance takes the smaller current: 12 ÷ 48 = 0.25 A.

parts.stem: Calculate the current through the 48 Ω resistor.
parts.workedSolution: I = 12 ÷ 48 = 0.25 A. Check: 0.5 + 0.25 = 0.75 A, the main-line reading.

hints: Q and R are equal and share the same two junctions.
parts.stem: A current of 540 mA flows through resistor P. State the current through resistor Q, in milliamps.
parts.workedSolution: 270 mA. Q and R are equal and have the same voltage across them, so the 540 mA splits evenly between them.

hints: All 540 mA passes through the S–T pair. S and T have the same voltage across them, so the smaller resistance takes the larger share.

commonErrors.feedback: Halving is only right for equal resistors, as Q and R were. S has half the resistance of T, so it takes twice T's current: 360 mA and 180 mA. The Summer 2023 Higher examiners saw only the most able split a current this way.
That gives S the smaller share. S has the smaller resistance, so it takes the larger current: 360 mA.

parts.stem: Calculate the current through resistor S, in milliamps.

scheme.for: S has half the resistance of T, so it takes twice the current: one share = 540 ÷ 3 = 180

parts.workedSolution: All 540 mA reaches the S–T pair. S (15 Ω) has half the resistance of T (30 Ω), so it takes twice the current: the currents are 2 : 1, three shares of 540 ÷ 3 = 180 mA. S takes two shares, 360 mA.

hints: The currents in S and T add up to the current through P.

commonErrors.feedback: S and T are not equal, so they do not take half each. T has twice the resistance, so it takes one share of three: 180 mA.
That is S's current. T has the larger resistance, so it takes the smaller share: 180 mA.

parts.stem: State the current through resistor T, in milliamps.
parts.workedSolution: 540 − 360 = 180 mA: the two branches add back to the 540 mA through P.

hints: Use the current through S, converted to amps, with the resistance of S.

commonErrors.feedback: The current went in as milliamps. V = I R needs amps: 360 mA = 0.36 A, so V = 0.36 × 15 = 5.4 V. Summer 2023 Higher candidates lost marks here by not converting 600 mA to 0.6 A.
That divides the current by the resistance. V = I R multiplies them: 0.36 × 15 = 5.4 V.

parts.stem:
Calculate the voltage across resistor S.
Show your working out.
parts.workedSolution: V = I R. 360 mA = 0.36 A, so V = 0.36 × 15 = 5.4 V. Check: T has the same voltage, 0.18 × 30 = 5.4 V.

hints: Take the bullets in order: series current, series voltage, parallel voltage, parallel current, then the two removals, then the house.

indicativeContent.point: in the series circuit the current is the same at every point, so the ammeter reads the same wherever it is placed
in the series circuit the voltages across the two lamps add up to the battery voltage, so each lamp has only part of it
in the parallel circuit each lamp has the full battery voltage across it
in the parallel circuit the current in the main line is the sum of the currents in the two branches
removing a lamp from the series circuit breaks the only loop, so the other lamp goes out
removing a lamp from the parallel circuit leaves the other branch complete, so the other lamp stays lit at the same brightness
house lights are wired in parallel so that each has the full mains voltage and each can be switched on or off without affecting the others

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A rule counts once it is stated as a comparison the reader could check with a meter: 'the current is the same everywhere' earns the series current point, 'the current is shared' does not. The two removal points are separate, and an answer that gives the same outcome for both circuits earns neither.

parts.workedSolution: In the series circuit there is one loop, so the current is the same at every point and the ammeter reads the same wherever it is placed. The voltages across the two lamps add up to the battery voltage, so each lamp has only half of it and is dim. In the parallel circuit each lamp is connected straight across the battery, so each has the full battery voltage across it and is at full brightness. The current in the main line is the sum of the currents in the two branches. If one lamp is removed from the series circuit the only loop is broken, so the other lamp goes out. If one lamp is removed from the parallel circuit the other branch is still complete, so the other lamp stays lit at the same brightness. House lights are wired in parallel so that every light has the full mains voltage, and each one can be switched on or off without affecting the others.

parts.stem:
Two identical lamps are connected to the same battery, first in series and then in parallel.
Which statement about the voltage across one lamp is correct?

options.text: in series the two lamps share the battery voltage; in parallel each lamp has the whole battery voltage
options.feedback: Yes. Series shares the supply out along the loop; parallel puts every branch straight across the battery.

options.text: in series each lamp has the whole battery voltage; in parallel the two lamps share it
options.feedback: That is the two rules swapped. In series the lamps are in one loop and share the supply; in parallel each branch is joined straight across the battery and has all of it.

options.text: each lamp has the same voltage in both circuits, because the battery is the same
options.feedback: The battery is the same, but the circuits use it differently: in series each lamp has half the battery voltage, in parallel each has all of it.

scheme.for: series: the lamps share the battery voltage; parallel: each lamp has the full battery voltage

parts.workedSolution: In series the two lamps share the battery voltage, so each has half of it; in parallel each lamp is joined straight across the battery and has the whole battery voltage.

hints: Think about what is true of the current at the battery in every circuit.
parts.stem: Which statement about the current is true of both circuits?

options.text: in both circuits the current leaving the battery is the current returning to it
options.feedback: Yes. Charge is never used up: whatever leaves one terminal comes back to the other, in series or in parallel.

options.text: the battery supplies the same current in both circuits
options.feedback: Not so: the parallel circuit gives the charge two routes, so it draws more current from the same battery than the series circuit does.

options.text: in both circuits the current halves as it passes each lamp
options.feedback: A lamp uses no current up in either circuit. In series the current is the same at every point; in parallel it splits between branches and adds back where they meet.

scheme.for: the current leaving the battery equals the current returning to it in both circuits (charge is not used up)

parts.workedSolution: In both circuits the current leaving the battery equals the current returning to it, because charge is never used up on the way round.

parts.stem: Explain why the lights in a house are connected in parallel, not in series.

accepted: Each light has the full mains voltage across it, and each light can be switched on or off without affecting the others.
Every lamp gets the full voltage so it works at full brightness, and one lamp can be switched off or fail without the others going out.

scheme.for: each light has the full (mains) voltage across it / works at full brightness
each light can be switched on or off (or can fail) without affecting the others

parts.workedSolution: Each light has the full mains voltage across it, so it works at full brightness. Each light is on its own branch, so it can be switched on or off, or can fail, without affecting the others.

findTheMistake.stem:
Niamh is asked: 'A 9 V supply drives a 10 Ω resistor and a 30 Ω resistor connected in parallel. The current in the main line is 1.2 A. Calculate the current in each resistor. [3]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Each branch has the supply voltage across it: 9 V
The two branches share the current equally: 1.2 ÷ 2 = 0.6 A
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The branches only share equally when their resistances are equal. These are 10 Ω and 30 Ω, so each branch's current is the voltage across it divided by its own resistance: 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9 A and 9 ÷ 30 = 0.3 A, which do add up to 1.2 A.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark of three: the voltage across each branch is right. The two current marks need each branch worked from its own resistance, 0.9 A and 0.3 A; halving is only for equal branches, which Summer 2023 Higher candidates managed while few managed this.

findTheMistake.stem:
Cara is asked: 'Resistor X, of resistance 25 Ω, is in series with two equal resistors Y and Z connected in parallel. A current of 40 mA flows through Y. Calculate the voltage across X. [4]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Z is equal to Y, so Z carries 40 mA
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: 80 is a number of milliamps, and V = I R needs the current in amps. 80 mA = 0.08 A, so V = 0.08 × 25 = 2.0 V. A small cell could never put 2000 V across one resistor, which is the sign a conversion was missed.
findTheMistake.feedback: Three marks of four: both currents in milliamps and the equation are right. The answer mark needs the current converted to amps before it goes into V = I R, the step Summer 2023 and Summer 2025 Higher examiners saw missed.

prompts.prompt: In a series circuit, how does the current at one point compare with the current at any other point?
prompts.answer: It is the same at every point.

prompts.prompt: In a series circuit, what do the voltages across the components add up to?
In a parallel circuit, what is the voltage across each branch?
prompts.answer: The supply voltage, on every branch.

prompts.prompt: In a parallel circuit, how is the current in the main line related to the branch currents?
prompts.answer: It is the sum of the branch currents.

prompts.prompt: How do you tell a series circuit from a parallel one?
prompts.answer: Trace the route: one route through everything is series; a route that splits at a junction is parallel.

prompts.prompt: Two unequal resistors are in parallel. Which one carries the larger current?
prompts.answer: The smaller resistance: both have the same voltage, and I = V ÷ R.
